claim: Scgn-expressing cells in rat dorsal striatum are interneurons that express NeuN but not Ctip2.
source: As in mice, Scgn-expressing cells in rat dorsal striatum were interneurons (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G,H demonstrating co-expression of Scgn with NeuN but not Ctip2.

claim: In rat dorsal striatum, about one half of Scgn+ interneurons also express PV.
source: Across all striatal sections, about one half of Scgn+ interneurons also expressed PV (Figure 1K, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by stereological cell counting data presented in Figure 1K and associated source data.

claim: In rat dorsal striatum, about one quarter of PV+ interneurons also express Scgn.
source: about one quarter of PV+ interneurons also expressed Scgn (Figure 1L, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by stereological cell counting data presented in Figure 1L and associated source data.

claim: Scgn+ interneurons in rat have a density that is about two thirds of that of PV+ interneurons.
source: Scgn+ interneurons were relatively common overall, with a density that was about two thirds of that of PV+ interneurons
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of cell density measurements from stereological counting.

claim: In mice, the vast majority of Scgn+ interneurons do not co-express PV.
source: However, interneurons that co-expressed PV and Scgn were rare. Indeed, the vast majority of Scgn+ interneurons did not co-express PV and vice versa (Figure 1C–F, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and stereological data shown in Figure 1C-F.

claim: All striatal Scgn+ cells in mice co-express the pan-neuronal marker NeuN but not the SPN-specific marker Ctip2.
source: All striatal Scgn+ cells co-expressed the 'pan-neuronal' marker NeuN, but not the SPN-specific marker Ctip2 (Arlotta et al., 2008) (Figure 1A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1A,B and cited reference for Ctip2 as SPN marker.

claim: The density of PV+/Scgn- interneurons in rat dorsal striatum remains relatively constant along the rostro-caudal axis until the most caudal aspects where density decreases by around 75%.
source: The density of PV+/Scgn- interneurons remained relatively constant along the rostro-caudal axis of dorsal striatum, at least until the most caudal aspects where density decreased by around 75% (Figure 2Ai,B, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by density measurements across coronal planes shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PV+/Scgn+ interneurons in rat display a strikingly different pattern of localization compared to PV+/Scgn- interneurons, being more sparsely distributed across most striatal levels except in the most caudal aspects where their density is around three times higher than that of PV+/Scgn- interneurons in any other plane.
source: However, PV+/Scgn+ interneurons displayed a strikingly different pattern of localization, being more sparsely distributed across most striatal levels, except in the most caudal aspects where their density was around three times higher than that of PV+/Scgn- interneurons in any other plane (Figure 2Aii,B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by density measurements and spatial distribution data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PV+/Scgn+ interneurons in rat tend to distribute more laterally in the rostral striatum but more medially in caudal striatum.
source: PV+/Scgn+ interneurons tended to distribute more laterally in the rostral striatum but more medially in caudal striatum (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by medio-lateral distribution analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PV+/Scgn- interneurons in rat are evenly distributed along the medio-lateral axis of the striatum.
source: The two populations of interneurons were also differentially distributed along the medio-lateral axis of the striatum; PV+/Scgn- neurons were evenly distributed
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial distribution analysis.

claim: PV+/Scgn- interneurons in rat are more likely than PV+/Scgn+ interneurons to display a slight dorsal bias in their localization.
source: Along the dorso-ventral axis, PV+/Scgn- interneurons were more likely than PV+/Scgn+ interneurons to display a slight dorsal bias in their localization (Figure 2D, Supplementary file 1, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by dorso-ventral distribution analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In rat dorsal striatum, the biased medio-lateral distributions of PV+ interneurons can be largely explained by the selective expression of Scgn.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that, in rat dorsal striatum, the biased medio-lateral distributions of PV+ interneurons can be largely explained by the selective expression of Scgn.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of distribution patterns between all PV+ interneurons and PV+/Scgn+ subpopulation.

claim: There is no consistent or strong bias in the relative positions of all PV+ interneurons in mouse dorsal striatum.
source: There was no consistent or strong bias in the relative positions of all PV+ interneurons in mice (Figure 2H)
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The distribution pattern of all PV+ interneurons in mice closely resembles that of PV+/Scgn- interneurons in rats.
source: their distribution pattern closely resembled that of PV+/Scgn- interneurons in rats (Figure 2G), but not that of all PV+ interneurons in rats (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of distribution patterns shown in Figures 2E, 2G, and 2H.

claim: About three quarters of PV+ interneurons in monkey caudate nucleus and putamen also express Scgn.
source: Compared to the rat, co-expression of PV and Scgn was more common in primates; about three quarters of PV+ interneurons in caudate nucleus and putamen also expressed Scgn (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by stereological cell counting data in monkey striatum shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is a marked increase in the density of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons in caudal planes of monkey striatum, most notably in the caudate nucleus.
source: Along the rostro-caudal axis of monkey striatum, but most notably in the caudate nucleus, there was a marked increase in the density of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons in caudal planes (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 2, Figure 3—source data 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by density measurements across coronal planes in monkey shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The density of PV+/Scgn- interneurons remains relatively constant across the rostro-caudal extent of monkey striatum.
source: The density of PV+/Scgn- interneurons remained relatively constant across the rostro-caudal extent of monkey striatum, which is again in line with our observations in rats (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 2, Figure 3—source data 1.).
evidence: The claim is supported by density measurements in monkey striatum shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The distribution of PV+/Scgn- interneurons, but not PV+/Scgn+ neurons, is laterally biased throughout rostro-caudal aspect of monkey putamen, but not caudate.
source: Interestingly, the distribution of PV+/Scgn- interneurons, but not PV+/Scgn+ neurons, was laterally biased throughout rostro-caudal aspect putamen, but not caudate (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 2, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by medio-lateral distribution analysis in monkey shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The action potential waveforms of all PV+ interneurons, irrespective of Scgn immunoreactivity, are brief (1.09 ± 0.06 ms).
source: In agreement with this, our recordings confirmed that the action potential waveforms of all PV+ interneurons, irrespective of Scgn immunoreactivity, were brief (1.09 ± 0.06 ms, n = 24; Figure 5A.).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and waveform analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The duration of the first deflection (D1) of the action potentials of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons (0.31 ± 0.014 ms) is significantly shorter than those of PV+/Scgn- interneurons (0.39 ± 0.02 ms).
source: Further analysis showed that the duration of the first deflection (D1) of the action potentials (see Figure 5A) of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons (n = 10 cells; 0.31 ± 0.014 ms) was significantly shorter than those of PV+/Scgn- interneurons (n = 14 cells; 0.39 ± 0.02 ms) (Mann Whitney, p=0.006).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements and statistical comparison (Mann Whitney test, p=0.006).

claim: The average firing rates of PV+/Scgn+ and PV+/Scgn- interneurons are similar during slow-wave activity (SWA).
source: Although the firing rates of PV+ interneurons as a whole could vary substantially (range: 0.01 – 22.52 spikes/s; see Figure 4) during SWA, the average firing rates of PV+/Scgn+ and PV+/Scgn- interneurons were similar in this brain state (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by firing rate measurements during SWA shown in Figure 5B.

claim: During cortical activation, the firing rate of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons (median = 13.8 spikes/s) is significantly higher than that of PV+/Scgn- interneurons (median = 3.74 spikes/s).
source: However, during cortical activation, the firing rate of PV+/Scgn+interneurons (median = 13.8 spikes/s) was significantly higher than that of the PV+/Scgn- interneurons (median = 3.74 spikes/s, Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.03; Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by firing rate measurements during cortical activation and statistical comparison (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.03).

claim: The ISI histograms of ChAT+ interneurons are significantly more positively correlated than those of PV+ interneurons during both SWA and cortical activation.
source: Across all recorded neurons, the ISI histograms of ChAT+ interneurons were significantly more positively correlated than those of PV+ interneurons during both SWA and cortical activation (Mann Whitney, SWA; p=0.001 × 10−37; Act: p<0.025 × 10−36)
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of ISI histograms with statistical comparison (Mann Whitney tests).

claim: During both SWA and cortical activation, the r-values for pairs of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons are significantly higher than those of PV+/Scgn- pairs.
source: During both SWA and cortical activation (Figure 5G,H, Figure 5—source data 1), the r-values for pairs of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons were significantly higher than those of PV+/Scgn- pairs (p<0.05 for both Kruskal–Wallis ANOVAs and post hoc Dunn's tests)
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis with statistical comparison (Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA and Dunn's tests, p<0.05).

claim: The r-values for pairs of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons are not significantly different from pairs of ChAT+ interneurons during both SWA and cortical activation.
source: the r-values for pairs of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons were significantly higher than those of PV+/Scgn- pairs (p<0.05 for both Kruskal–Wallis ANOVAs and post hoc Dunn's tests), but not significantly different from pairs of ChAT+ interneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis with statistical comparison.

claim: Both PV+/Scgn- and PV+/Scgn+ interneurons tend to fire around the peaks of cortical slow oscillations (0.4–1.6 Hz) during SWA.
source: As suggested by the raw data (Figure 4), both PV+/Scgn- and PV+/Scgn+ interneurons tended to fire around the peaks of cortical slow oscillations (0.4–1.6 Hz) during SWA (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by phase-locking analysis shown in Figures 4 and 6A,B.

claim: The locking of PV+/Scgn- interneurons to cortical slow oscillations during SWA is stronger than that of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons.
source: Although the firing of all PV+ interneurons was significantly locked to cortical slow oscillations to some extent (Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1), the locking across the population was stronger in the PV+/Scgn- neurons (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by phase-locking analysis shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: The vector length of firing of PV+/Scgn- interneurons to cortical slow oscillations during SWA is around twice that of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons.
source: In line with these results, the vector length of firing of PV+/Scgn- interneurons was around twice that of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons (Figure 6D; Mann Whitney, p=0.04).
evidence: The claim is supported by vector length measurements and statistical comparison (Mann Whitney, p=0.04).

claim: The firing of PV+/Scgn- interneurons is more strongly locked to cortical spindle oscillations (7–12 Hz) during SWA than PV+/Scgn+ interneurons.
source: Similarly, the firing of PV+/Scgn- interneurons was more strongly locked to cortical spindle oscillations (7–12 Hz), which was reflected in both a greater number of significantly locked neurons (Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1) and greater vector length (Figure 6D, Mann Whitney, p=0.008).
evidence: The claim is supported by phase-locking analysis with statistical comparison (Mann Whitney, p=0.008).

claim: The firing of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons is more tightly locked to cortical gamma (30–80 Hz) oscillations during SWA than PV+/Scgn- interneurons.
source: In contrast, the firing of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons was more tightly locked to cortical gamma (30–80 Hz) oscillations (Figure 6A,B), and a greater proportion of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons were significantly locked to gamma oscillations (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by phase-locking analysis shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Around three times as many PV+/Scgn+ interneurons are locked at gamma frequencies between 30 and 60 Hz during cortical activation as compared to PV+/Scgn- interneurons.
source: However, around three times as many PV+/Scgn+ interneurons were locked at gamma frequencies between 30 and 60 Hz as compared to PV+/Scgn- interneurons (Figure 6G, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phase-locking analysis during cortical activation shown in Figure 6G.

claim: 69.2 ± 2.4% of appositions made by the axons of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons with SPN somata are associated with discrete puncta of gephyrin immunoreactivity.
source: Indeed, 69.2 ± 2.4% of appositions (n = 104) made by the axons of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons (n = 3) with SPN somata were associated with discrete puncta of gephyrin immunoreactvity
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of gephyrin co-localization at apposition sites.

claim: 75.5 ± 6.6% of appositions made by the axons of PV+/Scgn- neurons with SPN somata are associated with discrete gephyrin+ puncta.
source: while 75.5 ± 6.6% of appositions (n = 94) made by the axons of PV+/Scgn- neurons (n = 2) were associated with discrete gephyrin+ puncta.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of gephyrin co-localization at apposition sites.

claim: Neurobiotin-labeled boutons of PV+/Scgn- interneurons are almost twice as likely as those of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons to appose the somata of SPNs.
source: Neurobiotin-labeled boutons of PV+/Scgn- interneurons (neurons = 4, boutons = 347) were almost twice as likely as those of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons (neurons = 3, boutons = 709) to appose the somata of SPNs (Figure 8C; Fisher Exact Test, p<0.001. Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of appositions with statistical comparison (Fisher Exact Test, p<0.001).

claim: SPN somata apposed to at least one axonal bouton of a PV+ interneuron receive a significantly greater number of appositions from the axons of PV+/Scgn- interneurons compared to appositions from the axons of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons.
source: A complementary analysis showed that SPN somata that were apposed to at least one axonal bouton of a PV+ interneuron received a significantly greater number of appositions from the axons of PV+/Scgn- interneurons (n = 46 SPN somata) as compared to appositions from the axons of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons (n = 44 SPN somata; Figure 8D, Mann Whitney, p=0.009. Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of appositions per SPN with statistical comparison (Mann Whitney, p=0.009).

claim: The axonal boutons of PV+/Scgn- interneurons are more commonly apposed to iSPN somata than to dSPN somata.
source: More specifically, the axonal boutons of PV+/Scgn- interneurons (n = 119 boutons from 4 interneurons) were more commonly apposed to iSPN somata than to dSPN somata (Figure 8A,E, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of appositions to PPE+ vs PPE- SPNs shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The axons of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons preferentially target dSPN somata.
source: In contrast, the axons of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons (n = 238 boutons from 4 interneurons) preferentially targeted dSPN somata (Figure 8B,E, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of appositions to PPE+ vs PPE- SPNs shown in Figure 8E.

claim: PV+/Scgn- and PV+/Scgn+ interneurons significantly differ in their preferential targeting of the somata of iSPNs and dSPNs.
source: Quantitative analysis confirmed that these two populations of PV+ interneurons significantly differed in their preferential targeting of the somata of iSPNs and dSPNs (Fisher Exact Test, p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of targeting preferences (Fisher Exact Test, p<0.0001).

claim: The median firing time of dSPNs significantly precedes that of iSPNs during SWA.
source: Accordingly the median firing time of dSPNs significantly preceded that of the iSPNs (Figure 9D, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of spike timing relative to iLFP peaks shown in Figure 9D.

claim: PV+/Scgn- interneurons fire significantly earlier than PV+/Scgn+ interneurons during SWA.
source: Analysis of median firing times confirmed that PV+/Scgn- interneurons fired significantly earlier than PV+/Scgn+ interneurons (Figure 9D, Figure 9—source data 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of spike timing relative to iLFP peaks shown in Figure 9D.

claim: PV+/Scgn- interneurons fire significantly earlier than iSPNs but not dSPNs during SWA.
source: it was evident that PV+/Scgn- interneurons fired significantly earlier than iSPNs but not dSPNs
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of firing times shown in Figure 9D.

claim: PV+/Scgn+ interneurons do not fire before iSPNs or dSPNs during SWA, and their firing is significantly delayed as compared to dSPNs.
source: whereas PV+/Scgn+ interneurons did not fire before iSPNs or dSPNs (their firing was significantly delayed as compared to dSPNs).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of firing times shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Unsupervised hierarchical cluster analysis of electrophysiological parameters during SWA segregates interneurons into 5 significant clusters.
source: When these 7 parameters were analyzed across all interneuron populations, 5 significant clusters emerged (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical cluster analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Two of the five clusters from hierarchical analysis during SWA are predominantly composed of cholinergic interneurons.
source: After assignment of molecular identities, it was evident that two of these clusters were predominantly composed of cholinergic interneurons (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cluster analysis with molecular identity assignment shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Three of the five clusters from hierarchical analysis during SWA are composed of a clear majority of PV+/Scgn-, PV+/Scgn+ or NOS+/NPY+ interneurons.
source: The three remaining clusters were composed of a clear majority of PV+/Scgn-, PV+/Scgn+ or NOS+/NPY+ interneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by cluster analysis with molecular identity assignment shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Unsupervised hierarchical cluster analysis of electrophysiological parameters during cortical activation segregates interneurons into 4 significant clusters.
source: When these 6 parameters were analyzed across all interneuron populations, 4 significant clusters emerged (Figure 10F).
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical cluster analysis shown in Figure 10F.

claim: The four clusters from hierarchical analysis during cortical activation are predominantly composed of cholinergic interneurons, NOS+/NPY+ interneurons, PV+/Scgn- interneurons or PV+/Scgn+ interneurons.
source: After assignment of molecular identities, it was evident that these clusters were predominantly composed of cholinergic interneurons, NOS+/NPY+ interneurons, PV+/Scgn- interneurons or PV+/Scgn+ interneurons (Figure 10F)
evidence: The claim is supported by cluster analysis with molecular identity assignment shown in Figure 10F.

claim: Striatal PV+ interneurons can form axo-somatic synapses with SPNs.
source: Striatal PV+ interneurons can form axo-somatic synapses with SPNs (Koos and Tepper, 1999; Kubota and Kawaguchi, 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PV+ interneurons powerfully inhibit SPNs of both the direct pathway and indirect pathway.
source: allowing them to powerfully inhibit SPNs of both the so-called 'direct pathway' and 'indirect pathway' (Gittis et al., 2010; Planert et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Striatal PV+ interneurons exhibit short-latency responses to powerful excitatory inputs from afferents originating in distinct cortical areas.
source: These interneurons exhibit short-latency responses to powerful excitatory inputs from afferents originating in distinct cortical areas (Ramanathan et al., 2002; Sharott et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PV+ interneurons provide a mechanism for rapidly stopping or delaying SPN spiking.
source: providing a mechanism for rapidly stopping or delaying SPN spiking (Mallet et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Physiologically-classified putative PV+ interneurons in striatum appear to have a specific role in 'selecting' motor programs, firing most intensely at the choice execution/decision making point of a given task.
source: Consistent with this, physiologically-classified (putative) PV+ interneurons in striatum, often called 'fast-spiking interneurons' (FSIs), appear to have a specific role in 'selecting' motor programs, firing most intensely at the choice execution/decision making point of a given task (Friedman et al., 2015; Gage et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Severe movement deficits result from the loss or selective disruption of striatal PV+ interneurons.
source: The functional importance of striatal PV+ interneurons is further illustrated by the severe movement deficits that result from their loss or selective disruption (Burguière et al., 2013; Gittis et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In cortical circuits, PV+ GABAergic interneurons comprise multiple cell types with distinct structural, neurochemical and physiological features.
source: In cortical circuits, PV+ GABAergic interneurons comprise multiple cell types with distinct structural, neurochemical and physiological features (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Striatal PV+ interneurons are usually treated as a single functionally-homogenous population that is enriched within dorsolateral striatum.
source: In contrast, striatal PV+ interneurons are usually treated as a single functionally-homogenous population that is enriched within dorsolateral striatum (Gerfen et al., 1985; Kita et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Striatal PV+ interneurons in rats can be broadly divided into two subtypes based on the sizes of their axonal and dendritic fields.
source: Striatal PV+ interneurons in rats can be broadly divided into two subtypes based on the sizes of their axonal and dendritic fields (Kawaguchi, 1993)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The ratio of synapses formed with SPN somata and dendrites varies considerably between individual PV+ cells.
source: and the ratio of synapses formed with SPN somata and dendrites varies considerably between individual PV+ cells (Kubota and Kawaguchi, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Identified PV+ interneurons in rats display highly variable firing rates and patterns in vivo.
source: Physiologically, identified PV+ interneurons in rats display highly variable firing rates and patterns in vivo (Sharott et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Almost half of all PV+ interneurons in mouse striatum express serotonin receptor subunit 3A.
source: Moreover, studies in mouse striatum indicate that almost half of all PV+ interneurons express serotonin receptor subunit 3A, again highlighting possible functional disparity (Munoz-Manchado et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Secretagogin is an EF-hand calcium-binding protein.
source: Secretagogin (Scgn), an EF-hand calcium-binding protein (Rogstam et al., 2007; Alpár et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Secretagogin is expressed by some sparsely distributed non-cholinergic striatal neurons.
source: as it is expressed by some (sparsely distributed) non-cholinergic striatal neurons (Mulder et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Ctip2 is a marker specific to striatal projection neurons (SPNs).
source: All striatal Scgn+ cells co-expressed the 'pan-neuronal' marker NeuN, but not the SPN-specific marker Ctip2 (Arlotta et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation establishing Ctip2 as SPN-specific marker.

claim: In the adult mouse, secretagogin is expressed by some GABAergic, but not cholinergic, striatal neurons.
source: In the adult mouse, the calcium-binding protein secretagogin (Scgn) is expressed by some GABAergic, but not cholinergic, striatal neurons (Mulder et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Secretagogin expression patterns may vary across species.
source: Secretagogin is expressed in many brain areas, and expression patterns may vary across species (Alpár et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Striatal afferents and efferents are topographically organized.
source: Striatal afferents (and efferents) are topographically organized (Mailly et al., 2013; McGeorge and Faull, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Caudal striatal territories in rats receive converging inputs from most areas of prefrontal, entorhinal, prelimbic, visual and auditory cortical areas.
source: These caudal striatal territories receive converging inputs from, in particular, most areas of prefrontal (Hoover and Vertes, 2011; Mailly et al., 2013), entorhinal (McGeorge and Faull, 1989), prelimbic (Mailly et al., 2013), visual (Faull et al., 1986) and auditory cortical areas (McGeorge and Faull, 1989; Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rostral and central territories of rat striatum receive denser and more widespread inputs from somatosensory and motor cortical areas.
source: On the other hand, in rostral and central territories of striatum, which receive denser and more widespread inputs from somatosensory and motor cortical areas, PV+/Scgn- interneurons outnumbered PV+/Scgn+ interneurons by at least 3:1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the statement about PV+/Scgn- predominance in rostral/central striatum combined with known corticostriatal organization.

claim: Combinations of afferents from prefrontal, association and visual cortices of primates innervate large areas of the caudate and putamen across most of their rostro-caudal axes.
source: In line with this change in relative cortical volume, combinations of afferents from prefrontal, association and visual cortices of primates innervate large areas of the caudate and putamen across most of their rostro-caudal axes (Calzavara et al., 2007; Haber and Knutson, 2010; Yeterian and Pandya, 1998)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Corticostriatal neurons in motor and somatosensory cortical areas of primates primarily target the lateral putamen.
source: whereas corticostriatal neurons in motor and somatosensory cortical areas primarily target the lateral putamen (Flaherty and Graybiel, 1991; Inase et al., 1996; Parent and Parent, 2006; Takada et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both rat caudal striatum and primate caudal caudate receive dense inputs from visual cortical areas.
source: Both rat caudal striatum (Faull et al., 1986) and primate caudal caudate receive dense inputs from visual cortical areas (Gattass et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In hippocampus, PV is expressed by at least four distinct types of GABAergic interneuron (axo-axonic, basket, bistratified and O-LM cells) that selectively innervate different compartments of target cells.
source: In hippocampus, PV is expressed by at least four distinct types of GABAergic interneuron (axo-axonic, basket, bistratified and O-LM cells) that selectively innervate different compartments of target cells (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Approximately 50% of PV-immunoreactive terminals in the striatum form symmetric synapses with putative SPN somata.
source: Approximately 50% of PV-immunoreactive terminals in the striatum form symmetric synapses with putative SPN somata (Bennett and Bolam, 1994; Kita et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some PV-immunoreactive terminals in striatum could originate from neurons in external globus pallidus.
source: While some of these terminals could originate from neurons in external globus pallidus (Bevan et al., 1998; Mallet et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A much larger proportion of PV-immunoreactive terminals in striatum are likely to originate from PV+ interneurons than from external globus pallidus.
source: a much larger proportion are likely to originate from PV+ interneurons (Koos and Tepper, 1999; Kubota and Kawaguchi, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In vitro electrophysiological recordings in mice suggest that PV+ interneurons provide either approximately equal inhibition to dSPNs and iSPNs, or have a slightly greater influence on dSPNs.
source: In vitro electrophysiological recordings in mice have suggested that PV+ interneurons provide either approximately equal inhibition to dSPNs and iSPNs, or have a slightly greater influence on dSPNs (Gittis et al., 2010; Planert et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The terminals of corticostriatal neurons show little selectivity for the two SPN populations.
source: The terminals of corticostriatal neurons show little selectivity for the two SPN populations (Doig et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2015; Kress et al., 2013; Wall et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PV+ interneurons have high sensitivity to cortical input.
source: The utility of this mechanism would be further enhanced by the high sensitivity of PV+ interneurons to cortical input (Gittis et al., 2010; Mallet et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Innervation of the somatic compartments of pyramidal neurons by some types of cortical PV+ interneurons is a key factor contributing to the role of these interneurons in the generation of network oscillations.
source: Innervation of the somatic compartments of pyramidal neurons by some types of cortical PV+ interneurons is a key factor contributing to the role of these interneurons in the generation of network oscillations (Freund and Katona, 2007; Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The strong temporal relationships between the firing of PV+ interneurons or FSIs to cortical oscillations is well described in striatum.
source: The strong temporal relationships between the firing of PV+ interneurons or FSIs to cortical oscillations is also well described in striatum (Berke, 2004, 2009; Sharott et al., 2012, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A recent study in mice demonstrated feedforward inhibition of SPNs in striosomes, but not matrix compartment, of rostro-medial striatum by afferents from prelimbic cortex.
source: A recent study in mice demonstrated feedforward inhibition of SPNs in striosomes, but not matrix compartment, of rostro-medial striatum by afferents from prelimbic cortex (Friedman et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Optogenetic manipulation of the prelimbic corticostriatal/inhibitory-interneuron pathway specifically altered performance in cost/benefit decision making.
source: Optogenetic manipulation of this corticostriatal/inhibitory-interneuron pathway specifically altered performance in cost/benefit decision making, illustrating that inhibitory interneurons can enable cortical afferents from a single area to selectively mediate a subset of striatal outputs (Friedman et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The caudal striatum of rats mediates the association of auditory stimuli with rewarding actions.
source: Consistent with this idea, the caudal striatum of rats has been shown to mediate the association of auditory stimuli with rewarding actions (Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Striatal PV+ interneurons have short duration (<1 ms) action potentials.
source: Striatal PV+ interneurons have short duration (<1 ms) action potentials (Mallet et al., 2005; Sharott et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Short action potential duration is a characteristic often used to putatively identify PV+ interneurons (as FSIs) in awake, behaving animals.
source: a characteristic often used to putatively identify them (as FSIs) in awake, behaving animals (Adler et al., 2013; Berke, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bursts of spikes in PV+ interneurons can considerably delay or even prevent SPN spiking.
source: Bursts of spikes in PV+ interneurons can considerably delay or even prevent SPN spiking, and inhibition mediated by PV+ interneurons is considerably stronger than that mediated by other GABAergic interneurons (Gittis et al., 2010; Koos and Tepper, 1999; Planert et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inhibition mediated by PV+ interneurons is considerably stronger than that mediated by other GABAergic interneurons.
source: and inhibition mediated by PV+ interneurons is considerably stronger than that mediated by other GABAergic interneurons (Gittis et al., 2010; Koos and Tepper, 1999; Planert et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gephyrin is highly enriched in the post-synaptic membranes of GABAergic synapses.
source: Whether or not these appositions indicated the presence of functional axo-somatic synapses between PV+ interneurons and SPNs was investigated by simultaneously detecting the presence of gephyrin, which is highly enriched in the post-synaptic membranes of GABAergic synapses (Sigal et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Somatic co-expression of DARPP-32 and preproenkephalin (PPE) identifies indirect pathway SPNs (iSPNs).
source: Somatic co-expression of DARPP-32 and preproenkephalin (PPE) was used to identify iSPNs, whereas those SPNs that did not express PPE were considered to be dSPNs (Ellender et al., 2011; Lee et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SPNs that do not express PPE are considered to be direct pathway SPNs (dSPNs).
source: whereas those SPNs that did not express PPE were considered to be dSPNs (Ellender et al., 2011; Lee et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The slow oscillation in the inverted striatal local field potential (iLFP) is a proxy signal for the cortically-driven synchronized 'up states' of many SPNs in the vicinity of the electrode.
source: The slow oscillation in the iLFP is of particular relevance because it is a proxy signal for the cortically-driven synchronized 'up states' of many SPNs in the vicinity of the electrode (Goto and O'Donnell, 2001; Stern et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Interneurons expressing NPY can be separated according to whether or not they also express NOS and/or somatostatin.
source: For example, interneurons expressing NPY can be separated according to whether or not they also express NOS and/or somatostatin; those expressing NPY, but not NOS, have a completely distinctive anatomical and physiological phenotype (Ibanez-Sandoval et al., 2011) and specific role in the microcircuit (English et al., 2012) as compared to NPY+/NOS+ interneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NPY+ interneurons that do not express NOS have a completely distinctive anatomical and physiological phenotype compared to NPY+/NOS+ interneurons.
source: those expressing NPY, but not NOS, have a completely distinctive anatomical and physiological phenotype (Ibanez-Sandoval et al., 2011) and specific role in the microcircuit (English et al., 2012) as compared to NPY+/NOS+ interneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mean volume of the dorsal striatum in rats is 23.2 ± 2.1 mm³.
source: When calculated in this manner across the striatum of 9 rats, the mean volume of the dorsal striatum was determined to be 23.2 ± 2.1 mm3.
evidence: The claim is supported by Cavalieri volume estimation from 9 rats.

claim: The mean volume of the dorsal striatum in mice is 9.40 ± 0.29 mm³.
source: In a similar manner, the mean volume of the dorsal striatum of 3 mice was calculated to be 9.40 ± 0.29 mm3.
evidence: The claim is supported by Cavalieri volume estimation from 3 mice.

claim: The calculated volume of rat dorsal striatum (23.2 ± 2.1 mm³) is similar to previous estimations.
source: This value is similar to previous estimations for the volume of the dorsal striatum in the rat (Oorschot, 1996; Rymar et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited previous studies.

claim: Corticostriatal afferents can engage parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) interneurons to rapidly curtail the activity of striatal projection neurons (SPNs), thus shaping striatal output.
source: Corticostriatal afferents can engage parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) interneurons to rapidly curtail the activity of striatal projection neurons (SPNs), thus shaping striatal output.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the overall findings of the study.

claim: The selective co-expression of secretagogin (Scgn) separates PV+ interneurons in rat and primate striatum into two topographically-, physiologically- and structurally-distinct cell populations.
source: We demonstrate that the selective co-expression of another calcium-binding protein, secretagogin (Scgn), separates PV+ interneurons in rat and primate striatum into two topographically-, physiologically- and structurally-distinct cell populations.
evidence: The claim is the main finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple lines of evidence throughout the manuscript.

claim: In rats, PV+/Scgn+ and PV+/Scgn- interneuron populations differ in their firing rates, patterns and relationships with cortical oscillations in vivo.
source: In rats, these two interneuron populations differed in their firing rates, patterns and relationships with cortical oscillations in vivo.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data presented in the Results section.

claim: The axons of identified PV+/Scgn+ interneurons preferentially target the somata of SPNs of the direct pathway.
source: Moreover, the axons of identified PV+/Scgn+ interneurons preferentially targeted the somata of SPNs of the so-called 'direct pathway'
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by anatomical data on axonal targeting.

claim: PV+/Scgn- interneurons preferentially target indirect pathway SPNs.
source: whereas PV+/Scgn- interneurons preferentially targeted 'indirect pathway' SPNs.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by anatomical data on axonal targeting.

claim: The two populations of PV+ interneurons (PV+/Scgn+ and PV+/Scgn-) could provide a substrate through which either of the striatal output pathways can be rapidly and selectively inhibited to subsequently mediate the expression of behavioral routines.
source: These two populations of interneurons could therefore provide a substrate through which either of the striatal output pathways can be rapidly and selectively inhibited to subsequently mediate the expression of behavioral routines.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the differential targeting of direct and indirect pathway SPNs.

claim: Scgn is a novel marker of a major class of striatal interneuron in the rat.
source: indicating that Scgn is itself a novel marker of a major class of striatal interneuron in the rat.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that Scgn+ interneurons have a density about two thirds that of PV+ interneurons.

claim: Scgn is a novel marker of a major class of striatal interneuron in monkeys.
source: Thus, Scgn is itself a novel marker of a major class of striatal interneuron in both monkeys and rats.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that about three quarters of PV+ interneurons in monkey striatum co-express Scgn.

claim: The divergence in Scgn immunoreactivity between rodent species is unlikely to be due to differences in antibody specificity.
source: We found this divergence in Scgn immunoreactivity between rodent species using two antibodies raised against different epitopes of Scgn that have 100% and 95% sequence homologies for rat and mouse, suggesting that the relative paucity of Scgn+ interneurons in mice was not a result of differences in antibody specificity (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the use of two different antibodies with high sequence homology to both rat and mouse Scgn.

claim: The particular pattern of bias in the distribution of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons in rat striatum has not been described for any other striatal cell population.
source: This particular pattern of bias in the distribution of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons is highly unusual in that it has not been described for any other striatal cell population.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with known distribution patterns of other striatal cell types.

claim: There is no quantitative evidence of a consistent 'dorsolateral' bias in the distribution of all PV+ interneurons in the striatum of rats.
source: However, in contrast to a previous report (Luk and Sadikot, 2001), we found no quantitative evidence of a consistent 'dorsolateral' bias in the distribution of all PV+ interneurons in the striatum of rats.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative spatial analysis and contrasts with a previous report.

claim: The discrepancy with a previous report of dorsolateral bias in PV+ interneuron distribution presumably arises from differences in cell-counting methodologies and analyses used.
source: This discrepancy presumably arises from differences in the cell-counting methodologies and analyses used, including the extent to which different regions of dorsal striatum were sampled; we calculated the relative position of each neuron counted in 13 coronal planes, rather than calculating cell densities according to arbitrary 'quadrants' in 1 coronal plane (Luk and Sadikot, 2001).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on methodological differences between studies.

claim: The amino acid sequence of Scgn is highly conserved across rats, mice, and primates.
source: We compared PV and Scgn expression across three species in which the amino acid sequence of Scgn is highly conserved (Gartner et al., 2007; Pruitt et al., 2014; Zierhut et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The somatosensory/motor cortical areas in primates comprise a far smaller fraction of the entire cortical mantle than in rodents, particularly in relation to prefrontal, association and visual cortical areas.
source: The somatosensory/motor cortical areas in primates comprise a far smaller fraction of the entire cortical mantle than in rodents, particularly in relation to prefrontal, association and visual cortical areas (Brodmann, 1909; Buckner and Krienen, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The relative switch in prevalence of the two PV+ interneuron populations between rats and primates is roughly in line with the relative difference in prevalence of somatosensory/motor corticostriatal projections versus prefrontal, associative, visual and auditory corticostriatal projections.
source: Thus, the relative switch in prevalence of the two PV+ interneuron populations in the two species is roughly in line with the relative difference in prevalence of somatosensory/motor corticostriatal projections versus prefrontal, associative, visual and auditory corticostriatal projections.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparison of interneuron distributions and known corticostriatal projection patterns.

claim: Neurons of the same cell type deliver identical neuroactive substances to a matching range of postsynaptic targets in the same temporal patterns.
source: Neurons of the same cell type deliver identical neuroactive substances to a matching range of postsynaptic targets in the same temporal patterns (Somogyi, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work defining cell type criteria.

claim: Cell type properties can be defined using molecular, structural and physiological features.
source: These properties can be defined using molecular, structural and physiological features (Petilla Interneuron Nomenclature et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to nomenclature guidelines.

claim: The findings describing the molecular profiles, distribution, structure and firing of striatal PV+ interneurons converge to suggest that striatal PV+ interneurons in rats and monkeys comprise at least two discrete cell types.
source: The findings presented here describing the molecular profiles, distribution, structure and firing of striatal PV+ interneurons converge to suggest that striatal PV+ interneurons in rats and monkeys comprise at least two discrete cell types.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the study.

claim: The unsupervised cluster analysis of PV+ interneuron firing during cortical activation suggests heterogeneity within PV+ interneurons may extend beyond two subtypes.
source: The unsupervised cluster analysis of PV+ interneuron firing during cortical activation suggested this heterogeneity may extend further.
evidence: The claim is based on cluster analysis results showing PV+/Scgn- interneurons divided into two clusters.

claim: A focus on mice as a model organism could potentially miss important substrates of interneuron diversity that are conserved along different phylogenetic paths.
source: However, this does not alter the likelihood that, although many elements of striatal circuits are likely conserved across mice, rats and primates, a focus on mice as a model organism could potentially miss important substrates of interneuron diversity that are conserved along different phylogenetic paths.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the species differences in Scgn expression observed in the study.

claim: PV+/Scgn+ interneurons are phylogenetically conserved to some extent between rats and primates.
source: When taken together, the data from monkey and rat not only show that a substantial proportion of striatal PV+ interneurons co-express Scgn, a population enriched in caudal striatum, but also that these novel constituents of the striatal microcircuit are phylogenetically conserved to some extent.
evidence: The claim is based on the finding of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons in both rats and primates with similar distribution patterns.

claim: Corticostriatal neurons in areas of rat cortex that heavily innervate caudal striatum could gain privileged access to PV+/Scgn+ interneurons.
source: Thus, corticostriatal neurons in areas of rat cortex that heavily innervate caudal striatum could gain privileged access to PV+/Scgn+ interneurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the enrichment of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons in caudal striatum and known corticostriatal projections.

claim: Corticostriatal neurons in 'somato-motor' areas of rat cortex are particularly well positioned to engage PV+/Scgn- interneurons.
source: Thus, corticostriatal neurons in 'somato-motor' areas of rat cortex are particularly well positioned to engage PV+/Scgn- interneurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the predominance of PV+/Scgn- interneurons in rostral/central striatum and known corticostriatal projections.

claim: The proliferation of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons in the macaque striatum could reflect the increase in decision-making capabilities required by the corticostriatal system of primates.
source: The proliferation of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons in the macaque striatum could reflect the increase in such decision-making capabilities required by the corticostriatal system of primates.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the higher proportion of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons in primates and their potential role in decision-making.

claim: PV+/Scgn+ interneurons may instantiate a mechanism whereby associative, visual and auditory cortical inputs can selectively inhibit dSPNs.
source: We propose that PV+/Scgn+ interneurons may instantiate a similar mechanism, whereby associative, visual and auditory cortical inputs can selectively inhibit dSPNs.
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on the preferential targeting of dSPNs by PV+/Scgn+ interneurons and their distribution.

claim: At the site of an apposition of a PV+ interneuron axonal bouton with a SPN soma, there is a high probability of a GABAergic synapse being formed.
source: These data suggest that, at the site of an apposition of a PV+ interneuron axonal bouton with a SPN soma, there is a high probability of a GABAergic synapse being formed.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high percentage (69-75%) of appositions associated with gephyrin puncta.

claim: An axon from an individual PV+ interneuron can form sufficient synaptic contacts to powerfully inhibit a single SPN.
source: Thus, in addition to several PV+ interneurons forming basket-like contacts with an SPN soma, our results indicate that an axon from an individual PV+ interneuron can form sufficient synaptic contacts to powerfully inhibit a single SPN.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that individual PV+ interneurons commonly form 2-4 putative synapses with a single SPN soma.

claim: The biased innervation of SPNs by two different types of PV+ interneuron may provide a novel mechanism through which corticostriatal neurons can selectively influence one or the other output pathway.
source: The biased innervation of SPNs by two different types of PV+ interneuron may, therefore, provide a novel mechanism through which corticostriatal neurons can selectively influence one or the other output pathway.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the differential targeting of dSPNs and iSPNs by PV+/Scgn+ and PV+/Scgn- interneurons.

claim: Selective innervation of iSPNs by PV+/Scgn- interneurons might explain why the firing of iSPNs was delayed compared to that of dSPNs.
source: Selective innervation of iSPNs by PV+/Scgn- interneurons might thus explain why the firing of iSPNs was delayed compared to that of dSPNs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the earlier firing of PV+/Scgn- interneurons relative to iSPNs and their preferential targeting of iSPNs.

claim: The relative timing of PV+/Scgn+ interneuron firing and dSPN firing would not be consistent with a powerful feedforward inhibitory circuit.
source: In contrast, the relative timing of PV+/Scgn+ interneuron firing and dSPN firing would not be consistent with a powerful feedforward inhibitory circuit.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that PV+/Scgn+ interneurons do not fire before dSPNs.

claim: The diverse properties of PV+/Scgn- and PV+/Scgn+ interneurons position them to fulfil different roles in the striatal circuit.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that the diverse properties of PV+/Scgn- and PV+/Scgn+ interneurons position them to fulfil different roles in the striatal circuit.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined anatomical and physiological differences between the two interneuron types.

claim: The firing of PV+/Scgn- interneurons is more likely to precede the firing of iSPNs than dSPNs.
source: When our observations are placed within a framework of feedforward inhibition in vivo, one might predict that, first, the firing of PV+/Scgn- interneurons is more likely to precede the firing of iSPNs than dSPNs
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the preferential targeting of iSPNs by PV+/Scgn- interneurons, which was subsequently validated by electrophysiological data.

claim: The firing of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons is more likely to precede the firing of dSPNs than iSPNs.
source: and secondly, that the firing of PV+/Scgn+ interneurons is more likely to precede the firing of dSPNs than iSPNs.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the preferential targeting of dSPNs by PV+/Scgn+ interneurons, which was not validated by electrophysiological data.
